title: Cutleaf Groundcherry in Rice Fields: How to Spot and Control It
metaTitle: Cutleaf Groundcherry in Rice: How to Identify and Control
metaDescription: Cutleaf groundcherry, or potokan, is an upright weed of rainfed rice fields. Learn to spot its yellow flowers and husked fruits and stop it before it seeds.
excerpt: Cutleaf groundcherry is an upright, branched broadleaf weed from the tomato family that farmers call potokan, sisiu or tino tino. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields, where it can rise above young palay. This page shows you how to spot it by its leaves, flowers and fruits, and how to control it before it drops seed.

heroImage.alt: Cutleaf groundcherry (Physalis angulata), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Cutleaf groundcherry belongs to the Solanaceae, the same family as tomato, eggplant and siling labuyo. Its local names include asisiu, kugut, potokan, sisiu, tutulakak and tino tino. It is a broadleaf weed with an upright, branching body. In the Philippines, you find it mostly in rainfed lowland rice fields, on soil that is not under water.

This weed is an annual. It sprouts, flowers, bears fruit and dies within one season, and it spreads only by seed. Each small fruit sits inside a papery husk and holds many tiny seeds. When the fruits fall and rot on the ground, those seeds wait in the soil and sprout with the next crop. So a few plants left standing now mean many more next season.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about cutleaf groundcherry
rows: Asisiu, kugut, potokan, sisiu, tutulakak, tino tino

blocks.text: Look for an upright, branched plant that rises among the rice hills. As a broadleaf, it has wide, flat leaves with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The leaves are oval to oblong, and the edges usually show uneven teeth, which gives the plant its English name. Its flowers are small and pale yellow. Later, each fruit hangs inside a papery husk that looks like a little lantern.

items: Upright, branched plants rising between the rice hills, sometimes above young palay.
Oval to oblong leaves with uneven, toothed edges and netted veins.
Small, pale yellow flowers that hang from the leaf joints.
Oblong to egg shaped fruits wrapped in a papery husk, like tiny lanterns.

blocks.text:
This weed grows tall and leafy, so it shades young palay and takes the light that rice needs. Its roots also draw water and fertilizer from the same soil. The damage hits hardest early, while the rice is still small.

Since it spreads only by seed, plants that escape weeding refill the soil with seed for next season. Its fruits can also end up mixed with harvested palay and dirty your grain. Besides, weedy patches give pests a place to hide between the rows.

items: Pull plants before the husked fruits form. Once fruits ripen and fall, each one adds many seeds to the soil.
Carry pulled plants with fruits out of the field, and do not leave them on the bunds to rot.
Keep water in the field when rain allows, because standing water keeps many land weeds like this from sprouting.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold cutleaf groundcherry down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Cutleaf Groundcherry Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Cutleaf Groundcherry

items.q: What is cutleaf groundcherry called in the Philippines?
items.a: Farmers give it several local names. You may hear asisiu, sisiu, kugut, potokan, tutulakak or tino tino, depending on the province. Its scientific name is Physalis angulata. It is a relative of tomato and eggplant, and its papery husked fruits make it easy to recognize once you know it.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first. Prepare the land well and use clean seed. Keep water in the field after planting when rain allows. Hand weed early, before fruits form, and take fruiting plants out of the field. If you need a herbicide, pick one by weed group and the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is cutleaf groundcherry harmful to my rice?
items.a: Yes, once it grows thick. It stands tall and shades young palay, and it takes water and fertilizer meant for the rice. It also fills the soil with seed if you let the fruits ripen. One plant may seem harmless, but a stand left until harvest turns into a bigger problem next season.
